item.title: “Do Gaz Zamin”: India’s last Mughal emperor died today 164 years ago; but his life of pain and tragedy lives
item.description: The man who was the last scion of India and South Asia’s most powerful ruling house, Bahadur Shah Zafar, died today 164 years ago in Rangoon (Yangon today), British-ruled Burma.
item.content:encoded:
“Do Gaz Zamin”: India’s last Mughal emperor died today 164 years ago; but his life of pain and tragedy lives The man who was the last scion of India and South Asia’s most powerful ruling house, Bahadur Shah Zafar, died today 164 years ago in Rangoon (Yangon today), British-ruled Burma. ANI | Updated: 07-11-2026 18:29 IST | Created: 07-11-2026 18:29 IST

the Red Fort, a magnificent 17th-century red sandstone structure in Delhi where mutinous Indian soldiers proclaimed the ageing and frail Mughal Emperor Bahadur Shah Zafar as ruler of India in May 1857. (Photo/REUTERS). Image Credit: ANI

Country:

India

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

The man who was the last scion of India and South Asia’s most powerful ruling house, Bahadur Shah Zafar, died today 164 years ago in Rangoon (Yangon today), British-ruled Burma. Zafar, the last emperor of the Mughal dynasty that ruled the subcontinent from 1526 to 1858, has become the symbol of the fickleness of power in popular imagination. Born to one of the strongest empires in human history, Zafar died alone and most importantly, far removed from the environs that he had called home throughout his life. Bahadur Shah was born on October 24, 1775, in Shahjahanabad, the Mughal citadel of Delhi that his illustrious ancestor, Shah Jahan, had built. His parents were Emperor Akbar Shah II and Lal Bai. Most know ‘Zafar’ as a poet, for the name was his takhallus. But to historians, Bahadur Shah’s life is also important while studying the Great Revolt of 1857, also known by other terms such as ‘The Sepoy Mutiny’ or ‘The First War of Indian Independence’, depending on which side of the fence one is on. The British East India Company had received permission to trade in the subcontinent from Zafar’s ancestor, Jehangir. Slowly, it developed into the strongest political force in the region until it became the de facto ruler. However, the Company Bahadur’s policies led to deep resentment. Things came to a head in 1857 when rumours of the cartridges of a brand new rifle for the Company’s Sepoys being laced with cow and pig fat began doing the rounds. On May 9, 1857, the soldiers in Meerut Cantonment revolted and rode towards Delhi. Crossing the Yamuna over a bridge of boats, they entered the city on May 11, where they declared the frail Zafar as the Shahenshah-e-Hind (Emperor of India/Emperor of Hindustan). Aged 82 and initially reluctant, Zafar lent his name, seal, and formal audience to the uprising, becoming its nominal head. After the British retook Delhi following a string of bloody battles in 1857, Major William Hodson captured Zafar and other members of the royal family on September 21, 1857, at Humayun's Tomb in Delhi, where they had sought refuge. A day later, Hodson shot and killed Zafar's sons, Mirza Mughal and Mirza Khizr Sultan, and grandson Mirza Abu Bakr in cold blood. The spot is now known ‘Khooni Darwaza’ and lies near Maulana Azad Medical College. As for Zafar, he was put on trial at the Red Fort and later exiled to Rangoon (Yangon, where he died in 1862 on November 7. It is in Rangoon that Zafar penned an immortal verse that has perhaps enshrined his memory among millions in the region: Kitna hai bad-naseeb 'Zafar' dafn ke liye, Do gaz zamin bhi na mili ku-e-yar mein. (English): How unfortunate is 'Zafar' for burial, Not even two yards of land were found in the beloved alley (referring to his homeland, Delhi). His life shows that even the most powerful dynasties cannot stand the march of Time and that only change is here to stay. Perhaps that is what makes the story of his life touching and appealing at the same time. (ANI)

item.title: FIFA partially upholds AFA's appeal against post World Cup sanctions; Nahuel's suspension reduced
item.description: As per Spanish newspaper Marca report quoted by Goal.com, FIFA cut the ban for Nahuel from seven matches to four and also reduced his fine from 90,000 dollars to 60,000. But for Parades, his 10-match ...
item.content:encoded:
FIFA partially upholds AFA's appeal against post World Cup sanctions; Nahuel's suspension reduced As per Spanish newspaper Marca report quoted by Goal.com, FIFA cut the ban for Nahuel from seven matches to four and also reduced his fine from 90,000 dollars to 60,000. But for Parades, his 10-match suspension along with his 90,000 dollar fine still stands.  ANI | Updated: 07-11-2026 14:41 IST | Created: 07-11-2026 14:41 IST

Argentina's Leandro Paredes clashed with Spain's Gavi after the match after Spain won the World Cup (Photo: Reuters). Image Credit: ANI

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

FIFA's Appeal Committee has partially upheld the Argentine Football Association (AFA) appeal against sanctions handed to several team members following the 2026 FIFA World Cup final, with Nahuel Molina's suspension getting reduced, while the punishment for midfielder Leandro Parades stands. As per a Spanish newspaper, Marca, report quoted by Goal.com, FIFA cut the ban for Nahuel from seven matches to four and also reduced his fine from 90,000 dollars to 60,000. But for Parades, his 10-match suspension along with his 90,000 dollar fine still stands. In an official statement, the AFA said that they would be requesting the grounds for decisions before taking them to the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS). AFA insists that they held "sufficient arguments from both a factual and legal standpoint" to demand a review of sanctions. Days after the World Cup final, the AFA was fined USD 321,000 for breaches of multiple articles of the FIFA Disciplinary Code (FDC), including the use of a sports event for demonstrations of a non-sporting nature, team misconduct, discrimination and racist abuse, and failure to ensure order and security at matches, according to the statement issued by FIFA's Disciplinary Committee. The sanctions were imposed in light of discriminatory chants and gestures by Argentina supporters during the tournament. In addition to the fine, the AFA was ordered to play its next two home matches with a limited number of spectators, allowing only 50 per cent attendance, due to the breach related to discrimination and racist abuse. FIFA further stated that USD 100,000 from the total fine must be invested in a plan aimed at combating discrimination. The governing body also confirmed that part of the sanction, including one of the two home-match restrictions and USD 100,000 of the fine, has been suspended with a probationary period. Meanwhile, following the report submitted by the Disciplinary and Ethics Prosecutor regarding incidents during the FIFA World Cup 2026 final between Spain and Argentina, FIFA also announced individual sanctions. Argentina players Paredes and Nahuel Molina received suspensions of 10 and 7 matches, respectively, along with fines of USD 90,000 each. Thiago Almada has been handed a one-match suspension and fined USD 30,000, while team official Roberto Ayala has been suspended for three matches and fined USD 30,000. Paredes, the Argentine midfielder, was involved in a post-match ruckus after Argentina's loss to Spain courtesy of an extra-time winner from Ferran Torres. Spain player Pablo Martin Paez Gavira also received a one-match suspension and a fine of USD 30,000. (ANI)

item.title: "Some things are best left unsaid": Darren Lehmann after Khawaja's explosive 2018 ball-tampering scandal claims
item.description: Khawaja has claimed that the entire Australian team, including players and support staff, was involved in the 2018 ball-tampering scandal during the South Africa tour. He said the responsibility was ...
item.content:encoded:
"Some things are best left unsaid": Darren Lehmann after Khawaja's explosive 2018 ball-tampering scandal claims Khawaja has claimed that the entire Australian team, including players and support staff, was involved in the 2018 ball-tampering scandal during the South Africa tour.  He said the responsibility was collective, contrary to Cricket Australia's findings that implicated only Steve Smith, David Warner and Cameron Bancroft. Khawaja stressed that he had expected the truth to emerge over the past eight years and spoke out to ensure the three players were not left carrying the blame alone.  ANI | Updated: 07-11-2026 13:53 IST | Created: 07-11-2026 13:53 IST

Usman Khawaja. (Photo: Reuters). Image Credit: ANI

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

Former Australian head coach Darren Lehmann questioned former batter Usman Khawaja's bombshell revelations about the 2018 ball-tampering scandal, saying that "somethings are best left unsaid sometimes for the good of the game and people". Khawaja has claimed that the entire Australian team, including players and support staff, was involved in the 2018 ball-tampering scandal during the South Africa tour.  He said the responsibility was collective, contrary to Cricket Australia's findings that implicated only Steve Smith, David Warner and Cameron Bancroft. Khawaja stressed that he had expected the truth to emerge over the past eight years and spoke out to ensure the three players were not left carrying the blame alone. Until now, the widely accepted account of the 2018 ball-tampering scandal, maintained by Cricket Australia (CA) and those involved, was that Steven Smith, David Warner and Cameron Bancroft were the only players responsible. Smith and Warner received 12-month bans from international and domestic cricket, while Bancroft was handed a nine-month suspension. Lehmann, who resigned from his position as head coach after the Sandpaper-Gate scandal, spoke on ABC Grandstand on Saturday after Khawaja's explosive claims about the whole team knowing the fact that a sandpaper had been used during the Cape Town Test in March 2018. "It has been an eventful morning, has not it? It just brings back really bad memories. It was a bad day in Australian cricket,” Lehmann said. “Everyone around the world was doing it, as people have spoken about. The extent of how much everyone knew, that is an individual case by case. For the families and the people involved, I feel for them right now because it is taking them back to a really bad place. It is a tough one, mate. It is not ideal at the start of the summer." “It is eight years ago, so some of the things you remember, some you do not," he added. Lehmann suggested that "some things were best left unsaid" as Khawaja made these revelations ahead of release of his autobiography titled 'Sabr' on Tuesday. He questioned if Khawaja could have said those things way back then. "Could he [Khawaja] have said this at the time [eight years]? I suppose that is one of the things in the book. Books are there to sell. He is retired. I have not spoken to Usman, to be fair. He has not texted me or rung me. That is just the way it is," he said. "I had to have a lot of help ... behind the scenes [after that incident]. It is not easy to talk about … but it puts you back in a bad place. Hopefully, I can get through this." "That is part and parcel of selling books, I suppose. I do not know what he is getting paid. He is probably getting paid a lot of money to do it. Is it worth it? I do not know. Maybe I write a book. Sometimes things are [best] left unsaid sometimes for the good of the game, and the good of the people," he continued. Asked on if the left-handed batter called for the team to take a collective responsibility after the scandal, Lehmann said that he dos not remember Khawaja doing so. "No, I do not remember that,” Lehmann said. “There were two change rooms [at the Cape Town venue] and meetings going on everywhere. I was in meetings with Cricket Australia a lot. I cannot remember that, but it could have been the case. That is what it is from his point of view," he said. “I do not think everyone would have known. But you do know ball tampering is going on because it has been happening for 150 years," he added. Lehmann also said that it is now upto the pace trio of Mitchell Starc, skipper Pat Cummins and Josh Hazlewood and spinner Nathan Lyon to speak to Khawaja. The revelations have renewed some scrutiny around these bowlers, who issued a joint statement back in 2021 denying that they were aware of a foreign substance being present on the field to alter the ball's conditions. "How much did they know? Only they know individually. They have been greats of the game. We are talking eight years ago. It is the Australian captain (Cummins). He has done a bloody good job over a long period of time," he signed off. Coming to Khawaja's statements, the southpaw had said to Nine as per Cricinfo, "It was all of us. Not the batters, not the bowlers, not the staff. All of us. In an ideal world, I don't want to do this. I don't want to be the one who comes out and talks about the truth. The issue is that I genuinely thought after eight years the truth would have been out by now." "Maybe I thought Davey would have exposed it, or someone else would have talked about it more. I just didn't think it was going to come down to this. But the longer it is gone on for, and right from the very start, I have been on the train of collectively taking it," he added. Khawaja said he had urged the Australian team to take collective responsibility for the 2018 ball-tampering scandal, insisting that everyone knew what was happening. He expressed disappointment that Smith, Warner and Bancroft were left to shoulder the blame, adding that Warner had faced repeated criticism over the past eight years while remaining silent. "Even in the change rooms when I was talking to them after the game. I said, 'Take this as a team'. We did this as a team. We knew what was going on, and we had to take it as a team, and so I was always of that stance. Obviously, it didn't work that way, and those three guys got crucified. I have seen Davey over the last eight years just get nailed bad over and over again, and it's taken a big man not to say anything and just to stay quiet," Khawaja added. Khawaja highlighted the lasting impact of the 2018 scandal on Cameron Bancroft and Steve Smith. He noted that Bancroft has struggled to regain his place in the Test side despite consistently scoring runs, while Smith successfully rebuilt his career but has never forgotten the events of that year. "And then 'Bangers' [Bancroft], in the same note, particularly, he played a little bit of Test cricket after that, but then never came back in, even though he's been scoring a lot of runs. He's been a terrific cricketer for a long time, but I know it's something that hangs over his head," Khawaja said. "Even Steve Smith. Steve's lucky, the greatest batsman of my generation. He came back from that, and he is come back as good as he ever was in that first Ashes series, and it is kind of been forgotten for him in some respects. But I know he has never forgotten that year and how it all panned out," he added. Khawaja said he spoke out because he believed Smith, Warner and Bancroft deserved justice and should not continue bearing the blame alone. He added that none of the three wanted to break their silence, fearing their accounts would be dismissed as hearsay, which prompted him to speak on their behalf. "But I am not doing this for any other reason than I think it is the right thing to do. I have always felt like there is more to life than just cricket, and these guys, in some respect, deserve that justice. And it just does not feel like anyone's going to give it to them. None of those three wants to be the first to say anything. And rightly so, it will just be hearsay and 'their word' if they do. They needed someone else to say something," he said. Khawaja also revealed that Cricket Australia never interviewed him during its investigation into the 2018 ball-tampering scandal. The probe, led by then head of integrity Iain Roy and team performance manager Pat Howard, followed the Cape Town Test and resulted in sanctions against Smith, Warner and Bancroft. "I was sitting next to Cam Bancroft that whole Test match, and I didn't get interviewed. I thoroughly feel that I didn't get interviewed because of that, because they knew that I wanted to take it as a team, because they knew I was ready to tell the truth if I was interviewed," he concluded. (ANI)

item.description: US President Donald Trump dismissed the ongoing conflict with Iran as "not a war", claiming significant progress and increased oil extraction. While defending past strikes against Iran's nuclear ...
item.content:encoded:
"Nobody hurt or killed in 5 months": Trump says US is not at war with Iran US President Donald Trump dismissed the ongoing conflict with Iran as "not a war", claiming significant progress and increased oil extraction. While defending past strikes against Iran's nuclear infrastructure, reports indicate that the true damage remains unclear, and Tehran maintains that its nuclear programme is peaceful. ANI | Updated: 07-11-2026 13:33 IST | Created: 07-11-2026 13:33 IST

US President Donald Trump (Photo/Reuters) . Image Credit: ANI

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

US President Donald Trump has described the ongoing confrontation with Iran as "not a war", claiming that Washington has made significant progress in dealing with Tehran and is currently extracting more oil than before the hostilities. "We made a lot of progress with Iran. We’re taking out more oil now than we were before the war. It’s not a war. It can’t be a war when for five months nobody was hurt, killed, or anything else. It’s not a war," Donald Trump said. These assertions come amid persistent ambiguity regarding the trajectory of the US military campaign targeting Iran, alongside ongoing deliberations concerning fresh air strikes. His contention that current tensions do not constitute a war persists despite White House deliberations regarding active military options, while broader friction with Tehran remains a primary regional concern. Furthermore, the American leader asserted that regional stability depended entirely on his administration's past interventions to obstruct Iranian atomic development. In a statement disseminated through his Truth Social platform, Donald Trump stated that his personal intervention against Iran’s nuclear ambitions remained universally recognised yet deliberately underreported. "Israel and, in fact, the entire Middle East, WOULD NOT EXIST TODAY if I did not stop Iran from having a Nuclear Weapon. Nobody wants to say that, but everybody knows it’s true!" he wrote. Trump has repeatedly portrayed operations directed at Iran’s nuclear infrastructure as an unqualified triumph. Both Washington and Israeli forces carried out extensive bombardments targeting Iranian nuclear and military facilities across 2025 and 2026, framing deterrence against the acquisition of atomic weapons as their core objective. Nevertheless, a full assessment of the damage sustained by Tehran's atomic enterprise remains inconclusive. A Congressional Research Service assessment published in October highlighted that the precise operational impact on indigenous weapons manufacturing capability remains undefined. The evaluation additionally emphasised past intelligence consensus indicating that Tehran had refrained from constructing atomic devices. Meanwhile, Iranian authorities persistently refute ambitions concerning nuclear weapons development, asserting that exclusively civilian applications govern their domestic atomic framework. (ANI)
